templates.description: The core recovery-test loop for a snapshot/point-in-time recovery tool: launch the environment in the recovery region from aligned recovery points, verify layer by layer, prove a business transaction, then triage everything you learned.
templates.whenToUse: Use for every Phase-1 recovery test with a snapshot-recovery tool (Arpio or similar). No DNS is touched and no live traffic moves — the success bar is a business transaction against the recovered stack via direct endpoints.
templates.name: Recovery test — snapshot recovery (Arpio-style)
preconditions: Phase 0 checklist is green and signed off
Recovery scope re-selected and saved in the recovery tool within the last week
Operator and approver both on the calendar for the full window
Agreed T0 definition written in the test plan (T0 = recovery launch initiated)

steps.title: Pre-flight: record T0 and recovery-point alignment
steps.detail: Open the test record. Write the wall-clock T0 the moment you initiate recovery. In the recovery tool, confirm the recovery points for ALL protected resources are aligned to the same point-in-time set (databases, S3, SQS, ECR from the same sync). Screenshot the recovery-point list — this is your RPA evidence.
steps.verify: Every in-scope resource shows a recovery point within the configured RPO window, all from the same sync set
steps.pass: Aligned recovery points, none older than RPO target; screenshot saved
steps.record: T0 timestamp; recovery-point ages per resource (this is RPA at T0)

steps.title: Pre-flight: confirm sandbox/network flags
steps.detail: Confirm the launch flags for a TEST: isolated/sandbox networking OFF where image pulls and secrets resolution need real egress (per your standing decision), and any 'do not touch production' guards ON. A test that launches with the wrong flags burns the whole window.
steps.verify: Flags match the documented test configuration in the test plan
steps.pass: Flags match; approver has seen them

steps.title: Launch ops/shared-services account first
steps.detail: Start recovery of the ops account (ECR registries, shared tooling) BEFORE the app account. App pods cannot start until their images exist in the recovery-region registry — ordering is not optional.
steps.verify: Recovery job for ops account running; ECR repositories appearing in recovery region
steps.pass: All ECR repositories present with expected image tags

steps.title: Launch application account
steps.detail: Start recovery of the application environment (VPC, EKS, databases, queues, buckets, secrets) from the aligned recovery points. Note the exact start time — cold-start duration is a number leadership will ask for.
steps.verify: Recovery job running; resources appearing in the recovery region in dependency order
steps.pass: Recovery job reports complete with zero failed resources
steps.record: App launch start/finish; any resources the tool reported as failed or skipped

steps.title: Verify platform: nodes, mesh, DNS, controllers
steps.detail: The cluster exists — now prove it is a platform. Nodes Ready, CoreDNS resolving, service mesh control plane up, load-balancer controller and autoscaler running. Do not look at app pods yet; a broken platform makes every app failure a red herring.
steps.command: kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -n kube-system && kubectl get pods -n istio-system
steps.verify: All nodes Ready; CoreDNS, istiod, ALB controller, Karpenter all Running
steps.pass: Platform pods healthy, no CrashLoopBackOff in system namespaces
steps.record: Node count, any system pods restarted manually

steps.title: Verify data layer: databases and queues restored
steps.detail: Connect to each restored database from inside the recovery VPC and run a freshness query (latest transaction timestamp). Compare against T0 — the difference is your measured RPA. Confirm queues exist; accept documented in-flight message loss.
steps.verify: Every database answers; latest-row timestamps within the recovery-point window
steps.pass: All databases reachable and fresh; RPA per database recorded
steps.record: Measured RPA (data age at T0) per database

steps.title: Verify secrets: every logical name resolves (tests usually die HERE)
steps.detail: This is the layer where recovery tests most often fail. Before starting apps, verify secrets-init (or your equivalent) can resolve EVERY logical secret name against the recovery-region Secrets Manager. One missing secret = crash-looping pods an hour later with a misleading error. Check the reconciled, signed-off secret list, not the list you hope is right.
steps.command: for s in $(cat signed-off-secrets.txt); do aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id "$s" --region <recovery-region> || echo "MISSING: $s"; done
steps.verify: Zero MISSING lines; secrets-init dry-run logs clean
steps.pass: Every logical name on the signed-off list resolves; no ResourceNotFoundException
steps.record: Any missing secrets → immediate finding, likely blocker

steps.title: Verify applications: pods up, images from recovery registry
steps.detail: Scale up / confirm app workloads. Check that pods are Running AND that their image references point at the RECOVERY-region registry, not the primary one (a pod pulling cross-region from the dead primary is a silent lie in a real event).
steps.command: kubectl get deploy -A && kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u
steps.verify: All Tier-0/1 deployments Ready; every image host is the recovery-region registry
steps.pass: Apps Ready; zero images referencing the primary region
steps.record: Time from launch to all apps Ready (cold-start number)

steps.title: Verify edge WITHOUT touching DNS
steps.detail: Prove reachability through the recovered API Gateway / load balancer using the DIRECT endpoint with a Host header matching the real domain. Public DNS is never changed in Phase 1 — the point is to prove the edge would work if it were.
steps.verify: HTTP 200 from the recovery edge; response comes from recovered backends
steps.pass: Healthcheck 200 with backend detail via direct endpoint + Host header

steps.title: Functional success bar: business transaction end-to-end
steps.detail: Run the agreed business transaction against the recovered stack (e.g. submit a test claim through the API and receive a real business response, not a 500). This — not green pods — is what 'recovered' means. Note the wall-clock time: first successful business transaction = T1.
steps.verify: Business-level success response with a real transaction id
steps.pass: Transaction answered end-to-end; T1 recorded; RTA = T1 − T0
steps.record: T1 timestamp; computed RTA in minutes

steps.title: Functional success bar: settlement/back-office path
steps.detail: Prove the second half of the bar: the settlement or batch path (e.g. remittance import runs against the recovered bucket/queue and writes to the recovered database). Front-door success with a dead settlement path is still an outage for finance.
steps.command: kubectl -n <ns> create job --from=cronjob/<settlement-import> test-import && kubectl logs job/test-import -f
steps.verify: Import job completes; rows land in the recovered database
steps.pass: Settlement path runs clean end-to-end

steps.title: Conclude: no failback without explicit approval
steps.detail: The test environment is torn down / recovery concluded ONLY on the approver's explicit go. Never trigger the tool's failback/teardown reflexively — in some tools failback has production side effects. Record who approved and when.
steps.verify: Written approval (chat message or ticket) from the named approver
steps.pass: Approval captured, then teardown executed
steps.record: Approver name, approval timestamp, teardown time

steps.title: Triage findings same-day: gaps, tickets, runbook edits
steps.detail: While it hurts, write the record: every surprise becomes (a) a gap with severity, (b) a ticket, or (c) an edit to this runbook — usually all three. A finding that lives only in someone's head is a finding you will rediscover during the real event.
steps.verify: Every finding in the test record has a gap id or ticket id next to it
steps.pass: Test record written same day; findings filed; runbook updated
steps.record: Findings list with severities and destinations

rollback.title: Tear down the recovered test environment
rollback.detail: After approval, conclude the recovery in the tool so test resources are destroyed and replication resumes toward the recovery region. Verify replication returns to green.
rollback.verify: Recovery-region test resources gone; replication status green again
rollback.pass: Tool shows protected + replicating; no orphaned resources billing in the recovery region
rollback.record: Teardown complete time; replication green time

templates.notes: Phase 1 never touches public DNS or live traffic. RTA/RPA measured here are the only honest numbers until a game day.

templates.description: Failover orchestrated by an ARC Region switch plan: execution blocks in dependency order (data switchover, compute scale-up, custom Lambda actions, Route 53 / routing-control flip), with approval gates and a monitored execution report.
templates.whenToUse: Use when AWS ARC Region switch (or a comparable orchestrator) owns the failover sequence. Requires the plan to already exist in BOTH regions and to have been exercised in practice mode — a plan first run during a disaster is a hypothesis, not a plan.
templates.name: Regional failover — Region switch plan
preconditions: Region switch plan exists and is healthy in BOTH regions (you trigger from the surviving one)
Plan has completed at least one practice-mode run in the last quarter
Execution role permissions verified in the recovery region
Decision-maker for the approval gate is reachable

steps.title: Confirm plan health and choose trigger region
steps.detail: Check the plan's evaluation status in the RECOVERY region console (assume the primary console is unavailable). Confirm the plan version matches the last practiced version — an un-practiced edit is a reason to pause.
steps.verify: Plan status healthy; version matches last practice run
steps.pass: Plan healthy in recovery region

steps.title: APPROVAL GATE: authorize failover execution
steps.detail: Real failover moves data-plane primaries and public traffic. The named decision-maker approves in writing (and via the plan's approval step if configured). Record the business reason and the declared incident.
steps.verify: Written approval captured; incident ticket open
steps.pass: Approval logged with timestamp
steps.record: Approver, timestamp, incident id — this is T0

steps.title: Trigger the plan (recovery-region console/CLI)
steps.detail: Start plan execution in real (not practice) mode from the recovery region. Note the execution id; everything from here is monitored through the execution report.
steps.verify: Execution started; execution id returned
steps.pass: Execution visible and progressing in the console

steps.title: Block: data switchover (Aurora Global etc.)
steps.detail: The plan's database block promotes the recovery-region replica (e.g. Aurora Global Database switchover/failover). Watch for the block to complete and confirm the new writer endpoint is in the recovery region. Managed switchover = zero data loss; unplanned failover = bounded loss (record it).
steps.verify: Writer is now the recovery-region cluster; replication reversed or pending
steps.pass: All database blocks complete; writers in recovery region
steps.record: Per-database switchover times; any data-loss window

steps.title: Block: compute scale-up (EKS / ASG / ECS)
steps.detail: The compute block scales recovery-region capacity from pilot-light to production size (node groups, ASG desired counts, ECS service counts). Watch for capacity errors — ICE/insufficient-capacity here is a known regional-event risk.
steps.command: kubectl get nodes | wc -l && kubectl get deploy -A # placeholder
steps.verify: Node/task counts reach production targets; workloads Ready
steps.pass: Compute block complete; apps Ready at production capacity

steps.title: Block: custom Lambda actions (app-specific steps)
steps.detail: App-specific glue the orchestrator can't know natively runs as custom Lambda execution blocks: warming caches, rotating partner credentials, re-pointing region-bound config, kicking batch schedulers. Each Lambda's success/failure shows in the execution report.
steps.verify: All custom action blocks report success in the execution report
steps.pass: No failed custom blocks

steps.title: Block: traffic flip (Route 53 health check / routing control)
steps.detail: The final block flips traffic: Route 53 health-check inversion, ARC routing control, or alias update. Confirm the change propagated and new connections land in the recovery region.
steps.verify: DNS answers point at recovery region; edge health 200
steps.pass: Traffic arriving in recovery region

steps.title: Monitor execution report to completion
steps.detail: Walk the full execution report: every block green, every step's duration logged. A yellow/skipped block is a finding even if traffic is flowing.
steps.verify: Execution status COMPLETED; no failed steps
steps.pass: Report saved into the test/incident record

steps.title: Verify functional success bar
steps.detail: Run the business transaction end-to-end in the recovery region (real customer path, not just health checks) plus the settlement/batch path. First success = T1; RTA = T1 − T0 (approval gate).
steps.verify: Business response with real transaction id; settlement path runs
steps.pass: Success bar met; T1 recorded

steps.title: Communications: stakeholders and partners
steps.detail: Announce failover completion to the incident channel, exec sponsor, and affected partners (they may see new egress IPs or brief errors). Keep the status page honest.
steps.verify: Comms sent per the comms plan; partner acks received
steps.pass: All notified parties acknowledged

rollback.title: Decide: fail back or stay
rollback.detail: Failing back is a SECOND failover with the same risks. Do not fail back on the day of the event unless forced. When the primary region is proven healthy, schedule failback as its own planned execution with its own approval.

rollback.title: Re-establish replication toward original primary
rollback.detail: Confirm Aurora Global (and any other replication) is streaming from the new primary back to the original region and lag is near zero before any failback plan runs.
rollback.verify: Replication healthy, lag seconds not hours

rollback.title: Execute the reverse plan (planned window)
rollback.detail: Failback = run the Region switch plan in the reverse direction during a quiet, announced window, with the same block-by-block verification as the failover.
rollback.verify: Reverse execution completes; traffic back on original primary
rollback.pass: Business transaction succeeds in original region

templates.notes: Practice-mode runs of the plan are the cheap rehearsal; do one per quarter minimum.

templates.description: Failover for stacks whose control plane (git + CI + IaC state) lives OUTSIDE the blast radius: fence the old primary, flip a single primary_region variable in git, apply, let reconciliation waves converge, promote data, verify parity, cut DNS. Rollback is the same flip reversed.
templates.whenToUse: Use when infrastructure is fully declarative (Terraform/Flux/Argo) and the deploy control plane demonstrably survives the primary region's loss. If CI or state storage lives in the failing region, fix that first — this runbook assumes it.
templates.name: Regional failover — GitOps primary_region flip
preconditions: Control plane (git host, CI runners, IaC state) confirmed healthy and outside the failing region
Both regions' stacks were green at last reconciliation
primary_region variable is the SINGLE switch — no hidden region-bound literals (verified by grep in CI)
Data replication (e.g. Aurora Global) healthy with low lag

steps.title: Preflight: both regions green in the deploy system
steps.detail: Check the CD dashboard: last reconciliation of BOTH region stacks succeeded. Failing over on top of a red recovery-region stack converts one incident into two.
steps.verify: Recovery-region stack reconciled and healthy; drift zero
steps.pass: Green in both regions (or documented known-red accepted by approver)
steps.record: Reconciliation timestamps both regions — approval here is T0

steps.title: Fence the old primary: disable writers (avoid split-brain)
steps.detail: Before promoting anything, make sure the old primary CANNOT accept writes even if it flickers back: scale writers to zero via the old region's stack if reachable, revoke DB security-group ingress, or disable the old writer endpoint. Split-brain is the one failure worse than downtime.
steps.command: kubectl --context <primary-ctx> scale deploy -n <ns> --all --replicas=0 # placeholder; if region unreachable, revoke SG ingress instead
steps.verify: No write traffic reaching old-primary database (connections drop to zero)
steps.pass: Old primary fenced or confirmed unreachable

steps.title: Flip primary_region in git
steps.detail: One commit: change primary_region from the failing region to the recovery region in the environment's variables file. PR with emergency approval per the incident process; merge. The commit SHA is your audit trail.
steps.command: git commit -am 'DR: primary_region <primary> -> <recovery>' && git push # via PR
steps.verify: Merged to the environment branch; CI pipeline triggered
steps.pass: Flip commit merged, pipeline running

steps.title: Apply and watch reconciliation waves converge
steps.detail: Terraform apply / Flux-Argo reconciliation now reshapes the recovery region into 'primary' (scale-ups, feature flags, schedulers on). Waves converge in dependency order — watch each wave, do not intervene manually unless a wave is truly stuck (manual edits create drift you'll pay for later).
steps.command: terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan # placeholder / flux reconcile ks --with-source
steps.verify: All applies/reconciliations complete without error; no perpetual-diff loops
steps.pass: Recovery region converged to primary configuration
steps.record: Apply duration per stack; anything applied out-of-band

steps.title: Promote data: managed database switchover
steps.detail: Promote the recovery-region database to writer (Aurora Global switchover if the old primary is alive — zero loss; failover if it is not — bounded loss, record the window). Update nothing by hand that the IaC already points at via region-neutral endpoints.
steps.verify: Writer endpoint now in recovery region; apps connect via the neutral endpoint
steps.pass: Writes succeeding in recovery region; no app pointing at old writer
steps.record: Switchover vs failover; data-loss window if any

steps.title: Run the parity/verification suite
steps.detail: Run the automated parity suite against the new primary: health endpoints, a synthetic business transaction, queue consumers draining, cron/batch schedulers active exactly once (in the NEW region only — double-running batch jobs is a classic split-brain leftover).
steps.verify: Suite green: business tx OK, consumers draining, schedulers single-region
steps.pass: Parity suite passes; first business success is T1
steps.record: Suite output; T1; RTA = T1 − T0

steps.title: Cut over DNS
steps.detail: Flip public DNS (alias/weighted records) to the recovery-region edge. With health-check-based records this may already have happened — verify rather than assume.
steps.verify: dig answers recovery-region targets; real traffic arriving and succeeding
steps.pass: Live traffic served by new primary

rollback.title: Rollback = the same flip, reversed
rollback.detail: The symmetry is the point: when the original region is healthy again, fence current writers, flip primary_region back in git, apply, promote data back, run the parity suite, cut DNS. Same runbook, opposite direction, in a planned window with its own approval.
rollback.verify: Same gates as failover, in reverse
rollback.pass: Parity suite green in original region; traffic cut back

templates.notes: The single-variable flip is only as real as your last grep for region-bound literals. Keep a CI check that fails on hardcoded regions.

templates.templateName: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) — EC2 workloads
templates.description: Failover for EC2/VM-based workloads using AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery: continuous block-level replication, drill vs recovery launches, right-sizing on launch, and reverse replication for failback.
templates.whenToUse: Use for lift-and-shift / EC2-based (or on-prem source) servers protected by AWS DRS. Not for containerized or managed-service stacks — those belong to the snapshot-tool or orchestrated runbooks.
templates.name: Failover — Elastic Disaster Recovery (EC2)
preconditions: All source servers show Healthy replication in the DRS console
Launch templates reviewed (subnet, SG, instance type) in the last month
Most recent drill completed successfully and instance right-sizing validated
IAM permissions for launch verified in the recovery region

steps.title: Verify replication health and lag
steps.detail: In the DRS console (recovery region), confirm every source server is CONTINUOUS with lag near zero and no stalled data. Lag now is data loss later — record it as your expected RPA.
steps.verify: All servers CONTINUOUS; lag under the RPO target
steps.pass: Replication healthy across the fleet
steps.record: Lag per server — expected RPA. Launch decision time is T0

steps.title: Choose launch type: DRILL vs RECOVERY
steps.detail: Drill launches are isolated and safe to run anytime; recovery launches are the real thing. Confirm with the approver which this is — the console buttons are adjacent and the difference is an outage report.
steps.verify: Written confirmation of drill vs recovery from approver
steps.pass: Launch type confirmed and recorded

steps.title: Launch recovery instances from latest point-in-time
steps.detail: Launch all servers (batch by dependency tier: data servers first, then app, then front-end) from the latest — or a chosen consistent — point in time.
steps.command: aws drs start-recovery --source-servers sourceServerID=<id1> sourceServerID=<id2> --is-drill <true|false> # placeholder
steps.verify: Recovery job running; instances entering 'launched' state
steps.pass: All instances launched without job errors

steps.title: Verify instance right-sizing and boot health
steps.detail: Check launched instance types against expected sizing (DRS right-sizing can pick a different family), OS boot success via instance screenshots/SSM, and disk mounts. An instance that boots but under-sized will fall over at real load.
steps.verify: SSM reachable on every instance; types match sizing sheet
steps.pass: All instances healthy and correctly sized

steps.title: Verify data volumes and application data freshness
steps.detail: On database/stateful servers: volumes mounted, services started, latest-transaction timestamps compared to T0 → measured RPA.
steps.command: ssm start-session --target <db-instance> # then check service + freshness query
steps.verify: Data services up; freshness within replication-lag expectations
steps.pass: Data layer verified; RPA recorded

steps.title: Start applications and verify service health
steps.detail: Start app services in dependency order, verify inter-server connectivity (SGs in the recovery VPC), and health endpoints.
steps.verify: All app health checks green
steps.pass: Application tier healthy

steps.title: Business transaction verification
steps.detail: Run the agreed business transaction against the recovered fleet (direct endpoint in a drill; through the real front door in a genuine failover). First success = T1.
steps.verify: Business-level success response
steps.pass: Success bar met; T1 and RTA recorded

steps.title: Drill only: terminate drill instances
steps.detail: For drills, terminate recovery instances via DRS (not raw EC2 terminate — let DRS clean up its jobs) once findings are captured. Replication continues untouched.
steps.verify: Drill instances gone; source servers still CONTINUOUS
steps.pass: Clean teardown, replication unaffected

rollback.title: Failback: reverse replication to original region
rollback.detail: After a real failover, start reversed replication (recovery instances become sources). Wait for CONTINUOUS with near-zero lag before scheduling failback.
rollback.verify: Reversed replication CONTINUOUS for all servers

rollback.title: Failback launch and traffic cutback
rollback.detail: In a planned window: quiesce writes, launch in the original region from the reversed replication, verify the business transaction, then cut DNS back. Same discipline as the failover.
rollback.verify: Business transaction succeeds in original region; DNS cut back
rollback.pass: Failback complete; replication re-reversed toward recovery region

templates.notes: DRS drills are cheap and isolated — run them monthly. The dangerous moments are launch-type selection and failback.

templates.description: The live exercise that wraps any failover runbook: real DNS flip, real partner transaction, real rollback plan, in a scheduled window with comms open and a decision-maker present. This is where RTO claims become real.
templates.whenToUse: Only after at least one clean Phase-1 recovery test. Use to exercise L7 (live cutover) with partners in the loop, inside an announced maintenance window, with a rehearsed rollback.
templates.name: Game day — live regional failover exercise
preconditions: A Phase-1 recovery test has passed cleanly within the last quarter
Maintenance window scheduled and announced to customers/partners
Partner has a named engineer on the bridge with a test transaction ready
Recovery-region egress IPs added to partner/edge allowlists IN ADVANCE
Rollback rehearsed on paper by the people who will execute it

steps.title: Open the bridge and comms channels
steps.detail: Open the incident bridge and the announcement channel at window start. Roll call: operator, approver/decision-maker, partner engineer, comms lead. No role present, no game day.
steps.verify: All named roles confirmed on the bridge
steps.pass: Roll call complete; window officially open

steps.title: Go/no-go: preflight checklist + rollback readiness
steps.detail: Walk the morning-of preflight checklist aloud. The decision-maker gives an explicit GO recorded in the decision log. Confirm the rollback steps are printed/open and the person executing rollback can state them from memory.
steps.verify: Preflight green; rollback owner recites the rollback plan
steps.pass: GO recorded — this is T0

steps.title: Execute the underlying failover runbook
steps.detail: Run the chosen failover runbook (snapshot recovery, Region switch plan, or GitOps flip) through its data/compute/app layers. This game-day runbook wraps it — keep both open; the game day adds the live-traffic edges around it.
steps.verify: Underlying runbook complete through its L6 verification
steps.pass: Recovery stack verified end-to-end via direct endpoints
steps.record: Which runbook, its own record link

steps.title: Confirm edge allowlists and certificates
steps.detail: Before flipping DNS: recovery egress IPs present in the partner's allowlist and the edge/WAF allowlist; certificate on the recovery edge valid for the public domain. Discovering an allowlist miss AFTER the flip means partner traffic dies publicly.
steps.command: openssl s_client -connect <recovery-edge>:443 -servername api.<your-domain> </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates # placeholder
steps.verify: Partner confirms allowlist entries; cert valid
steps.pass: Edge path verified pre-flip

steps.title: DNS flip to recovery region
steps.detail: Flip the public records (or trip the routing control / health-check inversion). Announce 'flip executed' on the bridge. Watch TTL-driven propagation; old-region traffic should decay over the TTL window.
steps.verify: dig from multiple resolvers answers recovery region
steps.pass: Public DNS answering recovery region

steps.title: Partner sends the LIVE test transaction
steps.detail: The partner engineer sends the agreed live transaction through the production front door. This single transaction is the whole point of the day: it proves DNS, edge, allowlist, auth, app, data — everything — with real partner traffic.
steps.verify: Partner receives the correct business response and confirms on the bridge
steps.pass: Live partner transaction answered — this is T1
steps.record: T1; RTA = T1 − T0; partner's transaction id

steps.title: Soak: watch live traffic and error budgets
steps.detail: Hold in the recovery region for the agreed soak period (e.g. 30-60 min). Watch error rates, latency, queue depths, settlement jobs. The decision-maker decides: extend, conclude, or roll back.
steps.verify: Error/latency within normal bands for the full soak
steps.pass: Soak clean; decision recorded

steps.title: Planned return: flip back per rollback plan
steps.detail: For an exercise, return to the primary region inside the same window using the rehearsed rollback (reverse DNS flip + underlying runbook's failback). Verify the business transaction in the primary region afterwards.
steps.verify: Traffic back on primary; partner transaction succeeds again
steps.pass: Return complete; both regions in their normal roles
steps.record: Return time; any surprises during rollback

steps.title: Close: comms, decision log, same-day record
steps.detail: Announce window close to all audiences. File every decision made on the bridge into the decision log. Write the game-day record the same day — including the ugly parts — and schedule the retro within a week.
steps.verify: Record written; retro scheduled; findings filed as gaps/tickets
steps.pass: Window closed cleanly with full paper trail

rollback.title: EMERGENCY rollback: reverse the DNS flip immediately
rollback.detail: If live traffic is failing after the flip and the fix is not obvious within the agreed patience window (e.g. 15 min), flip DNS straight back to the primary region FIRST, diagnose second. The primary is still healthy — that is what makes a game day safe.
rollback.verify: Traffic restored on primary; partner confirms success
rollback.pass: Customer impact ended; exercise findings captured
rollback.record: What failed, patience-window decision, rollback time

templates.notes: A game day without a rehearsed rollback is a production incident you scheduled yourself.
